messages.content: Write a Python decorator `retry` that re-runs a function on exception, with a maximum attempt count and exponential backoff. Around 40 lines.

`retry_exponential.py:6` — `retry(attempts, delay, backoff, max_delay, jitter, exceptions)`.

- Calls the function up to `attempts` times; the last failure's exception propagates.
- Wait starts at `delay` and multiplies by `backoff` each round, capped by `max_delay`.
- Jitter scales each sleep by a random factor in `[1 - jitter, 1 + jitter]` so simultaneous failures don't retry in lockstep.
- `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` always propagate, even under the default `exceptions=(Exception,)`.
- `functools.wraps` keeps the wrapped function's name and docstring.

Smoke test passed: a function failing twice then succeeding returned `"ok"` after 3 calls, and a function that always raises propagated its `RuntimeError`.

Note the repo already has near-identical implementations in `retry.py`, `retry_backoff.py`, and `retry_decorator.py` (all named `with_retries`) — I wrote a new file rather than overwrite any of them.

`retry_exponential.py:6` holds a `retry` decorator that re-runs a function when it raises, bounded by an attempt count and spaced by exponential backoff. Signature: `retry(attempts, delay, backoff, max_delay, jitter, exceptions)`. Roughly 40 lines.

- The function is called at most `attempts` times; if the final try fails, that exception is raised to the caller.
- The wait begins at `delay` and is multiplied by `backoff` after each failure, never exceeding `max_delay`.
- Each sleep is scaled by a random factor drawn from `[1 - jitter, 1 + jitter]`, so a group of callers that fail together does not come back in step.
- `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` are never swallowed, including under the default `exceptions=(Exception,)`.
- `functools.wraps` preserves the original name and docstring.

Smoke test: a function that fails twice and then succeeds gave back `"ok"` on the third call, and a function that raises every time let its `RuntimeError` through.

One thing to flag: `retry.py`, `retry_backoff.py`, and `retry_decorator.py` already contain close variants of this, each named `with_retries`. I added a new file instead of replacing any of them.

The `retry` decorator lives at `retry_exponential.py:6`. It re-runs a function whenever it raises, capped by an attempt count and spaced out with exponential backoff. Signature is `retry(attempts, delay, backoff, max_delay, jitter, exceptions)`, in about 40 lines.

- At most `attempts` calls are made; when the last one fails, its exception reaches the caller unchanged.
- Waiting starts at `delay`, gets multiplied by `backoff` after every failure, and stops growing at `max_delay`.
- A random factor from `[1 - jitter, 1 + jitter]` scales each sleep, so callers that failed at the same moment do not all retry at the same moment.
- `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` pass straight through, even with the default `exceptions=(Exception,)`.
- `functools.wraps` keeps the original function's name and docstring intact.

Smoke test: a function failing twice before succeeding returned `"ok"` on call three, and a function raising every time let its `RuntimeError` escape.

`retry_exponential.py:6` defines a `retry` decorator that calls a function again each time it raises, limited by an attempt count and paced by exponential backoff. The signature is `retry(attempts, delay, backoff, max_delay, jitter, exceptions)`, and it runs to roughly 40 lines.

- No more than `attempts` calls happen; if the final one fails, the caller sees that exception as-is.
- The wait opens at `delay`, grows by a factor of `backoff` after each failure, and is clamped at `max_delay`.
- Every sleep is multiplied by a random value in `[1 - jitter, 1 + jitter]`, so clients that fail together will not come back together.
- `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` are always re-raised, including under the default `exceptions=(Exception,)`.
- `functools.wraps` carries the original name and docstring over to the wrapper.

Smoke test: a function that failed twice and then worked returned `"ok"` on the third call, and a function that always raises let its `RuntimeError` reach the caller.

One caveat: `retry.py`, `retry_backoff.py`, and `retry_decorator.py` each already contain a near-identical version under the name `with_retries`. I created a new file instead of replacing any of those.
